name: Strategy & Cases
title: Case Cracker
blurb: Strategy consulting interviews in Japan test structured thinking, フェルミ推定 and case discussion in both languages, so this is the core skill set for Arin's first-choice role.

chapters.title: Structured thinking: MECE and issue trees
chapters.read: Study a consulting problem-solving primer's chapters on MECE, issue trees and hypothesis-driven work, plus any free consulting-club guide to 'logic trees' (ロジックツリー). Key ideas: break a question into non-overlapping, complete parts; lead with a hypothesis; apply the 'so what?' test.
chapters.produce: Build three issue trees (one profit question, one 'why' question, one 'how' question) at least three levels deep, and mark the branch you would test first with a one-line hypothesis.

quiz.q: What does MECE stand for?
opts: Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive
Measurable, Efficient, Clear, Exact
Mutually Exhaustive, Collectively Exclusive
Market, Economics, Competition, Execution
quiz.ex: MECE means the parts do not overlap (mutually exclusive) and together cover everything (collectively exhaustive).

quiz.q: You want to split a supermarket's customers by age. Which split is MECE?
opts: Students / Women / Over 60
Under 30 / 30-59 / 60 and over
Under 30 / 25-60 / Over 60
Young people / Office workers / Families
quiz.ex: Only the first split has no overlaps and no gaps: every customer falls into exactly one age band. The others overlap (a student can be a woman) or leave gaps.

quiz.q: In hypothesis-driven problem solving, what do you do early in the project?
opts: Collect every available data set before forming any view
Wait for the client to tell you the answer, then confirm it
State a best-guess answer and design analyses that would prove or disprove it
Choose a framework and fill in every box before thinking about the answer
quiz.ex: A hypothesis focuses the work: you test the most likely answer first instead of boiling the ocean, and revise it as evidence comes in.

quiz.q: A client asks 'Why are our profits falling?' Which first split of the issue tree is the most useful and MECE?
opts: Problems in Japan vs. problems with new products
Management problems vs. employee problems vs. customer problems
Marketing issues vs. pricing issues vs. sales issues
Revenue is falling vs. costs are rising
quiz.ex: Profit = revenue - cost, so 'revenue down' and 'cost up' are complete and non-overlapping at the first level. The other splits overlap or leave gaps.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the 'so what?' test when you review a finding?
opts: To check that the numbers add up to 100%
To check that the finding leads to a clear implication or action for the client
To make sure the slide has a chart on it
To confirm that the finding came from a reliable data source
quiz.ex: A fact alone ('sales in Kanto fell 12%') is not enough; 'so what?' pushes you to the implication ('so we should fix the Kanto store format first').

quiz.q: Your analysis shows that your first hypothesis was wrong. What should you do?
opts: Treat it as progress: update the hypothesis and the issue tree, then test the next most likely branch
Keep looking for data until the original hypothesis is supported
Abandon the issue tree and start collecting data without a hypothesis
Report to the client that the problem cannot be solved
quiz.ex: Disproving a hypothesis eliminates a branch. Hypothesis-driven work is iterative: you revise and move on, not defend the first guess.

chapters.title: Business frameworks: 3C, 4P, five forces, value chain
chapters.read: Read a strategy textbook's chapters on Porter's five forces and the value chain, and a Japanese marketing primer's sections on 3C分析 and 4P (マーケティング・ミックス). Key idea: frameworks are checklists for building a tailored structure, not answers to recite.
chapters.produce: Apply 3C, 4P and five forces to one Japanese company you know (e.g. a konbini chain) on a one-page sheet each, ending each page with one 'so what' line.

quiz.q: What are the three Cs in 3C analysis?
opts: Cost, Cash, Capital
Customer, Channel, Cost
Customer, Competitor, Company
Company, Country, Currency
quiz.ex: 3C analysis looks at the customer (market), competitors and the company itself to find where the company can win.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the 4Ps of the marketing mix?
opts: Product
Price
Promotion
Profit
quiz.ex: The 4Ps are Product, Price, Place and Promotion. Profit is an outcome, not a marketing lever.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of Porter's five forces?
opts: Government regulation
Threat of substitutes
Bargaining power of buyers
Rivalry among existing competitors
quiz.ex: The five forces are rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, buyer power and supplier power. Regulation can affect the forces but is not one of them.

quiz.q: Buyers of a product face high switching costs (changing supplier is expensive and slow). What does this do to buyer power?
opts: It raises buyer power
It has no effect on buyer power
It turns buyers into new entrants
It lowers buyer power
quiz.ex: If switching is costly, buyers cannot easily threaten to leave, so their bargaining power is weaker.

quiz.q: In Porter's value chain, which of these is a support activity rather than a primary activity?
opts: Inbound logistics
Operations
Human resource management
After-sales service
quiz.ex: Primary activities are inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service. HR management, technology development, procurement and firm infrastructure are support activities.

quiz.q: An interviewer asks: 'Should our client, a beverage maker, launch a sports drink?' What is the best way to use frameworks?
opts: Recite all five forces in order, then all 4Ps
Build a structure tailored to the question, borrowing relevant pieces (customer demand, competitors, client capabilities, economics)
Pick one framework and refuse to add anything outside it
Skip structure and start brainstorming ideas immediately
quiz.ex: Interviewers reward structures that fit the question. Frameworks are a source of ideas, not a script.

chapters.title: Profitability trees
chapters.read: Study a case-interview guide's chapter on profitability, plus a 簿記3級 or management-accounting textbook's section on fixed vs. variable costs and contribution margin. Key ideas: Profit = (Price - Variable cost) x Volume - Fixed cost; segment before you conclude.
chapters.produce: Draw a full profitability tree for a ramen chain and fill it with made-up but consistent numbers, then write a three-line diagnosis of where profit leaked.

quiz.q: For a ramen shop, which cost is variable (changes with the number of bowls sold)?
opts: Monthly shop rent
The manager's fixed monthly salary
Noodles and soup ingredients
Depreciation of the kitchen equipment
quiz.ex: Ingredients rise with each bowl sold. Rent, a fixed salary and depreciation stay the same whether you sell 100 or 300 bowls.

quiz.q: A ramen shop sells 300 bowls a day at ¥900. Variable cost is ¥350 per bowl and fixed costs are ¥120,000 per day. What is the daily profit in yen?
Same shop: price ¥900, variable cost ¥350 per bowl. What is the contribution margin ratio, in %? (one decimal place)
A company's sales volume rises 20% while its average price falls 10%. By what % does revenue change? (use a minus sign for a fall)
quiz.ex: Revenue = price x volume. 0.9 x 1.2 = 1.08, so revenue rises 8%. You cannot just add -10% and +20%.

quiz.q: Total revenue is flat, but you suspect a problem is hidden inside. Why do you segment revenue by product, channel and region?
opts: Because segmenting always makes the total revenue larger
To avoid having to look at costs at all
Because clients prefer longer slides
To find where the change is concentrated, since a flat total can hide a big fall in one segment offset by growth in another
quiz.ex: Averages and totals hide mix effects. Segmenting locates the specific product, channel or region where action is needed.

quiz.q: You found that a factory's cost per unit rose 15%. What is the best way to judge whether this is a real problem?
opts: Compare cost per unit with the company's own history and with competitors, and split it into its drivers
Assume it is fine because inflation exists
Look only at total revenue
Ask the factory manager if he is happy
quiz.ex: A number needs a benchmark (past, competitors) and a breakdown (materials, labour, overhead) before you can call it a problem.

chapters.title: Market sizing (フェルミ推定)
chapters.read: Work through a Japanese フェルミ推定 workbook's opening chapters and a case guide's market-sizing section. Key ideas: choose demand-side (population down) or supply-side (stores x capacity), segment the population, keep round numbers, and sanity-check with a second method.
chapters.produce: Solve 10 Fermi problems on paper in under 5 minutes each (e.g. konbini coffee cups per year in Japan), showing the tree and a sanity check for each.

quiz.q: Estimate annual rice-cooker sales in Japan. Inputs: 50 million households; 90% own a rice cooker; a rice cooker is replaced every 8 years on average. How many million units are sold per year?
quiz.ex: Owners = 50m x 0.9 = 45m. Replacements per year = 45m / 8 = 5.625m units.

quiz.q: Estimate annual konbini coffee revenue. Inputs: 55,000 stores; 120 cups per store per day; 365 days; ¥130 per cup. What is the revenue in ¥ billion? (one decimal place)
quiz.ex: 55,000 x 120 = 6.6m cups a day. x 365 = 2,409m cups a year. x ¥130 = ¥313.17bn, about ¥313.2bn.

quiz.q: Which approach is a supply-side estimate?
opts: Population x share who buy x purchases per year
Number of stores x customers each store can serve per day x days open
Number of households x ownership rate / replacement cycle
Number of office workers x share who buy lunch x working days
quiz.ex: Supply-side estimates start from the sellers' capacity (stores, seats, machines). The other three start from the buyers, which is demand-side.

quiz.q: How many hair salons does a city need? Inputs: 180,000 residents; each gets a haircut 6 times a year; a salon serves 12 customers a day and is open 300 days a year. How many salons?
quiz.ex: Demand = 180,000 x 6 = 1,080,000 haircuts a year. One salon = 12 x 300 = 3,600 a year. 1,080,000 / 3,600 = 300 salons.

quiz.q: You estimated a market at ¥5 trillion and it feels too large. What is the best next step?
opts: Present it anyway; Fermi answers cannot be checked
Sanity-check it with a different method or a known anchor (e.g. compare with total retail sales or a similar market)
Divide it by 10 so it feels more reasonable
Add more decimal places to make it more precise
quiz.ex: A second approach or a known anchor shows whether an assumption is off by an order of magnitude, and you can then fix that specific assumption.

quiz.q: Estimate the weekday bento lunch market. Inputs: 8 million office workers; 30% buy a bento on a working day; 240 working days a year; ¥600 per bento. What is the market size in ¥ billion? (one decimal place)
quiz.ex: 8m x 0.3 = 2.4m bentos a day. x 240 = 576m a year. x ¥600 = ¥345.6bn.

chapters.title: Mental math for cases
chapters.read: Practise with a case-math drill book or free case-math drill sites: percentages, growth rates, CAGR, break-even, the rule of 72, and handling zeros (万, 億, million, billion). Key idea: round sensibly, say your steps aloud, and state units.
chapters.produce: Do 15 minutes of timed case math daily for two weeks and log your speed and accuracy; finish with a self-made sheet of 30 problems at 90%+ accuracy.

quiz.q: What is 15% of 4,800?
Revenue grew from ¥80m to ¥92m. What is the growth rate in %?
Using the rule of 72, about how many years does it take for a value to double at 8% annual growth?
quiz.ex: Rule of 72: 72 / 8 = 9 years.

quiz.q: A product sells for ¥2,000 with a variable cost of ¥1,400 per unit. Fixed costs are ¥36 million a year. How many units must be sold to break even?
Sales grew from 100 to 121 over 2 years. What is the compound annual growth rate (CAGR) in %?
Operating margin rose from 8% to 10%. Which statement is correct?
opts: Margin rose by 2%, which is the same as 2 percentage points
Margin rose by 25 percentage points
Margin rose by 20%, which is 2 percentage points
Margin rose by 2 percentage points, which is a 25% increase in the margin
quiz.ex: 10 - 8 = 2 percentage points. As a relative change, 2 / 8 = 25%. Mixing up % and percentage points is a common case mistake.

chapters.title: Case types: profitability, market entry, growth
chapters.read: Read a case-interview book's chapters on profitability, market entry and growth cases, and practise with free case books from university consulting clubs. Key ideas: tailored structure, entry modes (build, buy, partner), the Ansoff matrix, payback.
chapters.produce: Run six full practice cases (two of each type) with a partner or out loud alone, recording each and writing a one-paragraph self-review.

quiz.q: In a profitability case you find raw-material costs rose 25% while other costs were flat. What is the best next step?
opts: Break the increase into price per kg vs. quantity used, and check whether competitors saw the same rise
Conclude immediately that the client should raise prices by 25%
Go back and re-check whether revenue was flat
Recommend firing the procurement team
quiz.ex: Drill into the driver: is it market price (likely industry-wide) or usage/waste (client-specific)? The competitor check tells you which.

quiz.q: Market entry: the target market is worth ¥50 billion. The client expects a 4% share by year 3 at a 10% net margin. What is the expected year-3 profit in ¥ million?
Entering the market costs ¥600 million up front and is expected to earn ¥150 million profit a year. What is the simple payback period?
quiz.ex: 600 / 150 = 4 years (simple payback, no discounting).

quiz.q: Which set of questions best structures a market entry case?
opts: What are revenue and costs this year compared with last year?
Who are our suppliers and how much do we pay them?
Is the market attractive? Can we win against competitors? Do we have the capabilities? How should we enter, and do the economics work?
What is our share price and dividend policy?
quiz.ex: Market entry needs market attractiveness, competition, client fit, entry mode (build, buy, partner) and economics. The first option alone is a profitability structure.

quiz.q: In the Ansoff matrix, selling a new product to your existing customers is called:
opts: Market penetration
Market development
Diversification
Product development
quiz.ex: Existing market + new product = product development. Existing/existing is penetration, new market/existing product is market development, new/new is diversification.

quiz.q: Which of these is an inorganic growth option?
opts: Opening new stores with the company's own money
Acquiring a regional competitor
Launching a new product line developed in-house
Raising prices on existing products
quiz.ex: Inorganic growth comes from acquisitions or mergers. The others grow the existing business from within (organic).

chapters.title: Case types: M&A and PE due diligence, pricing, operations
chapters.read: Study a case guide's chapters on M&A, private-equity due diligence, pricing and operations, plus a corporate-finance primer's pages on EV/EBITDA multiples. Key ideas: enterprise vs. equity value, cost vs. revenue synergies, MOIC, value-based pricing, bottlenecks.
chapters.produce: Write a one-page due-diligence checklist for a PE buyer of a Japanese regional supermarket chain, and solve one pricing and one operations case with full numbers.

quiz.q: In M&A, which kind of synergy is usually harder to achieve and treated more cautiously by buyers?
opts: Cost synergies from closing duplicate head offices
Cost synergies from combined purchasing volume
Revenue synergies, such as cross-selling to each other's customers
Cost synergies from merging IT systems
quiz.ex: Revenue synergies depend on customer behaviour the buyer does not control, so they are less certain than cost savings the buyer can execute.

quiz.q: A target has EBITDA of ¥2 billion. Similar companies trade at 8x EV/EBITDA. The target has net debt of ¥5 billion. What is its implied equity value in ¥ billion?
quiz.ex: EV = 2 x 8 = ¥16bn. Equity value = EV - net debt = 16 - 5 = ¥11bn.

quiz.q: A PE fund invests ¥10 billion of equity and sells its stake 5 years later for ¥25 billion. What is the multiple of invested capital (MOIC)?
Which describes value-based pricing?
opts: Setting the price based on how much value the product creates for the customer and what they are willing to pay
Adding a fixed markup to the unit cost
Matching the price of the closest competitor
Setting the lowest price that keeps the factory running at full capacity
quiz.ex: Value-based pricing starts from customer value. The others are cost-plus, competitor-based and capacity-driven pricing.

quiz.q: A product sells 10,000 units at ¥1,000 with a variable cost of ¥600. If the price rises to ¥1,100, volume falls to 8,500 units. By how many yen does total contribution change? (use a minus sign for a fall)
A production line has three stations in sequence with capacities of 60, 45 and 80 units per hour. The line runs 16 hours a day. What is the maximum daily output?
quiz.ex: The bottleneck is the slowest station: 45 units an hour. 45 x 16 = 720 units a day.

chapters.title: Chart reading and clear slides
chapters.read: Study a business-presentation or data-storytelling book's chapters on action titles, chart choice and slide layout, and look at public investor-relations decks to see consulting-style slides. Key ideas: one message per slide, title states the takeaway, chart type fits the comparison.
chapters.produce: Rebuild three messy slides (from any public deck or your own work) into consulting style with action titles, and make one waterfall chart in Excel or PowerPoint.

quiz.q: Which slide title is the best consulting-style action title?
opts: Profit analysis
Profit fell ¥1.2bn mainly because Kanto store sales dropped
FY results: data overview
Sales, costs and profit by region
quiz.ex: An action title states the takeaway in one sentence, so the reader gets the message without studying the chart. The others are only topic labels.

quiz.q: You want to show monthly revenue over the last three years. Which chart is usually best?
opts: A line chart
A pie chart
A radar chart
A table of 36 numbers with no chart
quiz.ex: Line charts show trends over time clearly. Pie charts suit a few parts of one whole at one moment.

quiz.q: Which chart best shows how profit moved from last year to this year, step by step through each driver (price, volume, costs)?
opts: A pie chart
A scatter plot
A waterfall (bridge) chart
A stacked area chart
quiz.ex: A waterfall starts at last year's value, adds and subtracts each driver as floating bars, and ends at this year's value.

quiz.q: A bar chart shows regional sales: A = 120, B = 80, C = 50, D = 30. What share of total sales does region A have, in %? (one decimal place)
A bar chart's y-axis starts at 95 instead of 0, and bars of 97 and 99 look very different. What is the problem?
opts: Nothing; axes should always start near the smallest value
The bars should be 3D to fix it
The chart should use more colours
The truncated axis exaggerates a small difference
quiz.ex: Bar length encodes value, so bar charts should start at zero. Starting at 95 makes a 2% gap look huge.

quiz.q: What is the main rule for the content of one consulting slide?
opts: As much data as possible so the client sees all the work
One main message per slide, supported by the chart and a few points
At least three different charts per slide
A different font for each section to keep it interesting
quiz.ex: A slide should prove one message stated in its title. Extra content dilutes the message.

chapters.title: Japanese industry knowledge
chapters.read: Read industry overviews in a 業界地図-style annual guide and the 'business overview' pages of large companies' integrated reports (統合報告書) for autos, electronics, 商社, convenience stores, banking and energy. Focus on structure: business models, value chains, key players and their roles, not this year's numbers.
chapters.produce: Write a one-page industry card for each of the six industries (value chain, how money is made, key players, two structural issues) and present one aloud in 3 minutes.

quiz.q: In the Japanese auto industry, what does 系列 (keiretsu) usually describe?
opts: A government agency that sets car prices
A type of car loan offered by banks
A rule that cars must be made only in Japan
Long-term, tiered supplier networks around an automaker, often with close ties such as shareholdings
quiz.ex: Automakers work with tiers of suppliers in long-term relationships; group companies supply key components and share engineering work.

quiz.q: How do 総合商社 (general trading companies) make much of their profit today?
opts: Only from fees for translating business documents
Mainly from retail bank deposits
From investing in and managing businesses across many sectors, not only from trading commissions
Only from government subsidies
quiz.ex: Trading houses moved from pure intermediary trading toward owning stakes in businesses (resources, food, retail, infrastructure) and earning investment income from them.

quiz.q: Which describes the typical business model of a major Japanese convenience store chain?
opts: Most stores are run by franchisees; headquarters earns fees from them and provides brand, logistics, products and IT systems
Every store is owned and staffed directly by headquarters
Stores are run by local governments
Headquarters earns money mainly by renting parking spaces
quiz.ex: Japanese konbini chains are mostly franchised. HQ's strengths are merchandising, private-brand products, frequent delivery logistics and data systems.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of Japan's three 'megabank' groups?
opts: Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG)
Japan Post Bank
Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group (SMBC Group)
Mizuho Financial Group
quiz.ex: The term 'megabanks' refers to MUFG, SMBC Group and Mizuho. Japan Post Bank is very large in deposits but is a separate, postal-origin bank.

quiz.q: What is distinctive about Japan's electricity grid?
opts: The whole country runs at 60 Hz
Every prefecture has its own frequency
Eastern Japan runs at 50 Hz and western Japan at 60 Hz, which limits power transfer between them
Japan imports most of its electricity through undersea cables from Korea
quiz.ex: The east/west frequency split dates from early equipment imports and means power must pass through frequency converter stations.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the long-term shift at many large Japanese electronics makers?
opts: Exiting B2B to focus only on televisions
Moving all production from overseas back into Japan
Stopping all research and development
Moving from mass-market consumer products toward B2B areas such as components, industrial systems and IT services
quiz.ex: Facing price competition in consumer electronics, many groups shifted toward higher-margin B2B businesses (e.g. image sensors, infrastructure, industrial equipment, IT).

chapters.title: Running a case interview in Japanese and English
chapters.read: Watch firms' public case-interview example videos and read a case guide's chapter on communication; build a phrase list in both languages (clarifying, asking for time, signposting, closing). Key ideas: clarify first, think aloud with structure, synthesise with the answer first.
chapters.produce: Run four mock cases (two in Japanese, two in English) with a friend or career centre, record them, and write a 30-second closing synthesis for each.

quiz.q: What should you do first after the interviewer gives you the case?
opts: Restate the question and objective, and ask a few clarifying questions
Immediately start calculating the market size
Present your final recommendation
Ask the interviewer which framework to use
quiz.ex: Restating and clarifying ensures you solve the right problem (e.g. the client's objective, timeframe, metric) before structuring.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to ask for time to structure your thoughts in a Japanese case interview?
opts: 「ちょっと待って。」
「考えさせろ。」
「少しお考えください。」
「少し考える時間をいただいてもよろしいでしょうか。」
quiz.ex: 「時間をいただいてもよろしいでしょうか」 is polite and natural. 「ちょっと待って」 is casual, 「考えさせろ」 is rude, and 「お考えください」 asks the interviewer to think.

quiz.q: Which structure is best for the closing synthesis?
opts: Recommendation first, then two or three supporting reasons, then risks and next steps
A chronological story of everything you analysed
A list of all the numbers you calculated
Background first, then analysis, with the recommendation saved for the final sentence
quiz.ex: Executives want the answer first. Lead with the recommendation, support it, and show judgement with risks and next steps.

quiz.q: What does 「結論から申し上げますと」 mean?
opts: "Let me explain the background first..."
"I have no conclusion yet..."
"To give you the conclusion first..."
"Please tell me your conclusion..."
quiz.ex: 結論 = conclusion, から = from, 申し上げる = humble 'say'. It signals an answer-first statement.

quiz.q: The interviewer hands you a data table. After reading it, what should you say?
opts: Read every number in the table aloud
The key insight and what it means for your hypothesis, e.g. 'Costs per store rose 20%, so the profit problem is on the cost side; I'd like to look at what drove it.'
Say 'Thank you' and wait for the next question
Ask the interviewer what the table means
quiz.ex: Interviewers test whether you can extract the 'so what' and link it back to your structure.

quiz.q: Halfway through, you realise you made a calculation error a minute ago. What is the best response?
opts: Say so calmly, correct it, and explain whether it changes your conclusion
Hide it and hope the interviewer did not notice
Apologise many times and ask to restart the case
Blame the interviewer for unclear data
quiz.ex: Catching and fixing your own error shows reliability. Consultants are judged on self-correction, not on never making mistakes.

boss.q: Estimate new-car demand. Inputs: 54 million households; 70% own a car; a car is replaced every 9 years on average (ignore first-time buyers and multi-car households). How many million cars are sold per year?

A gym charges ¥8,000 per member per month. Variable cost is ¥2,000 per member per month and fixed costs are ¥3.6 million per month. How many members does it need to earn a monthly profit of ¥1.2 million?
boss.ex: Contribution per member = ¥6,000. Needed contribution = 3.6m + 1.2m = ¥4.8m. 4,800,000 / 6,000 = 800 members.

boss.q: A company cuts its price from ¥500 to ¥450. By what % must volume increase to keep revenue unchanged? (one decimal place)
boss.ex: Revenue constant means volume x 450 = old volume x 500, so volume must rise by 500/450 - 1 = 0.111, about 11.1%.

boss.q: A Japanese konbini chain asks whether to enter Vietnam. Which first level of the issue tree is most MECE and decision-focused?
opts: Young customers / Office workers / Foreign tourists / Food
Marketing / Sales / Promotion / Advertising
Is the market attractive? / Can we win against competitors? / Do we have the capabilities? / Do the economics work?
Revenue in Japan / Costs in Japan / Japanese competitors
boss.ex: The first option covers each condition needed for a 'go' decision without overlap. The others mix categories, overlap (sales vs. promotion) or look at the wrong country.

boss.q: A PE fund buys a company at 5x EBITDA of ¥2bn (EV ¥10bn), funded with ¥4bn equity and ¥6bn debt. After 5 years, EBITDA is ¥3bn, the exit multiple is 6x and debt has been paid down to ¥2bn. What is the MOIC on the equity?
boss.ex: Exit EV = 3 x 6 = ¥18bn. Exit equity = 18 - 2 = ¥16bn. MOIC = 16 / 4 = 4.0x.

boss.q: A market grew from ¥200 billion to ¥292.82 billion over 4 years. What is the CAGR in %?
A small bento maker sells most of its output to one of the big konbini chains. Using five forces from the bento maker's point of view, which force is strongest?
opts: Bargaining power of suppliers
Bargaining power of buyers
Threat of substitutes
Threat of new entrants into konbini retail
boss.ex: A few large chains buying from many small makers can push prices and terms hard, so buyer power is high for the bento maker.

boss.q: A plant can make 1,200 units a day but makes 900. Fixed costs are ¥1.8 million a day. By how many yen does fixed cost per unit fall if output rises to full capacity?
Which closing synthesis is the strongest?
opts: 「いろいろ分析しましたが、どれも大事だと思います。」
「まず市場規模を計算し、次に競合を見て、そのあとコストを見ました。」
「データが足りないので、結論は出せません。」
「結論として、A社は東南アジアへ提携で参入すべきです。理由は、市場の成長性と提携先の物流網の二点です。リスクは規制で、次のステップとして現地調査を提案します。」
boss.ex: The first answer gives the recommendation, two reasons, a risk and a next step. The others are vague, only list what was done, or avoid a conclusion.

boss.q: A new machine replaces the customer's current option, which costs ¥8 million. The new machine also saves the customer ¥3 million a year in labour for 5 years (ignore discounting). What is its economic value to the customer (EVC) in ¥ million?
boss.ex: EVC = price of the next-best alternative + value of differentiation = 8 + 3 x 5 = ¥23m. Value-based pricing would set a price between ¥8m and ¥23m.
